# Leviticus 11:25–47 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## Overview of Sources Found

The most detailed verse-by-verse treatments came from **Enduring Word (David Guzik)**, **Ellicott’s Commentary**, **The Pulpit Commentary**, **Calvin’s Commentary**, and the **Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges**. Gill’s Exposition and Precept Austin provided briefer cross-reference-based notes. The **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** and **Calvin** offered tradition-specific perspectives. I was unable to fetch pages for Catholic/Orthodox, modern scholarship (NET Bible, Bible Odyssey), or Lutheran-specific sources within the tool limits.

---

## Verses 24–28: Disposal of Carcasses of Unclean Animals

**v. 25 —** Ellicott explains that the person who carries (“beareth”) the carcass out of the camp or city contracts a higher degree of defilement than one who merely touches it; therefore he must wash his clothes as well as his body. During the Second Temple period, the administrators of the law ruled that wherever Scripture says “wash his clothes,” it includes bathing the whole body — omitted here only “for the sake of brevity.” The Samaritan text and some Hebrew manuscripts actually contain the fuller phrase “wash his clothes and bathe himself in water.” Ellicott notes an allusion to Revelation 7:14, where the saints “washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” [Ellicott on Lev 11:25](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-11.html)

Gill similarly observes that “pollution by bearing or carrying is greater than that by touching” — the carrier must wash both clothes and body. He adds that saints who have contracted pollution from sin must “wash their garments and make them white in the blood of the Lamb.” [Gill on Lev 11:25](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/11.htm)

The Cambridge Bible notes that vv. 24–25 serve as a “general introduction” to the section, with “by these” referring forward to the animals described in vv. 26–30. Carrying part of the carcass involves “uncleanness of a higher degree than that caused by mere contact.” [Cambridge Bible on Lev 11](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/leviticus/11.htm)

**v. 26 —** Ellicott records a fascinating historical controversy: this verse was a point of dispute between Pharisees and Sadducees. The Pharisees held that “them” in “whoever touches them” refers only to *dead* carcasses of unclean animals — living unclean animals (camels, horses, donkeys) could be freely used for daily life (riding, labour). The Sadducees insisted the verse meant touching even *living* unclean animals defiled a person. The Pharisees’ reading prevailed as the national norm, making ordinary life far more manageable. The Authorised Version captures this by inserting “the carcases” in italics. [Ellicott on Lev 11:26](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-11.html)

**v. 27 —** The Pulpit Commentary identifies “whatsoever goeth upon his paws” as animals that have no hoofs but move stealthily — beasts of prey of the cat family, and also dogs. This adds a further mark of unclean animals beyond the hoof-and-cud rule. [Pulpit on Lev 11:24–28](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

The Cambridge Bible concurs: animals like the dog and cat, “whose feet are hand-like in form, having digits and claws,” are meant. [Cambridge Bible on Lev 11:27](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/leviticus/11.htm)

**v. 28 —** See notes on v. 25: carrying the carcass requires washing clothes and uncleanness until evening — the higher degree of defilement.

David Guzik (Enduring Word) observes that this system meant dead unclean animals couldn’t simply be left to rot; they had to be disposed of. The person doing the disposal underwent washing and a brief quarantine. Guzik notes that when the Black Death killed a quarter of Europe in the 1300s, many Jewish communities were largely spared because they followed these hygienic practices — though tragically this led to their being accused of causing the plague. [Enduring Word on Lev 11:24–28](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-11/)

---

## Verses 29–30: Reptiles and Creeping Things Named

**vv. 29–30 —** The Pulpit Commentary states that the Hebrew words translated “tortoise, ferret, chameleon, lizard, snail, mole” probably denote different varieties of lizard. The mouse is mentioned alongside “eating swine’s flesh and the abomination” in Isaiah 66:17, showing its association with idolatrous practices. These are “creeping things that creep upon the earth” — creatures that go on their belly but lack wings (unlike the flying insects of vv. 20–23). [Pulpit on Lev 11:29–30](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

Guzik notes that this list includes mammals (mole, mouse) as well as reptiles; the mammals are already excluded by the criteria of vv. 1–8 but are repeated here for clarity alongside the reptiles. [Enduring Word on Lev 11:29–30](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-11/)

---

## Verses 31–38: Transmission of Uncleanness from Carcasses

**v. 31 —** The principle is restated: touching the dead body of any of these swarming things causes uncleanness until evening.

**v. 32 —** The Cambridge Bible envisions “one of these small animals creeping into a pan or bag or garment, and being found dead.” In such a case, washable items (wood, clothing, leather, sackcloth) must be put in water and remain unclean until evening. [Cambridge Bible on Lev 11:32](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/leviticus/11.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary adds that the phrase translated “ranges for pots” in v. 35 (KJV) more accurately means “covered pots” — kettles with lids. [Pulpit on Lev 11:31–38](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

**v. 33 —** A clay (earthenware) vessel into which an unclean carcass falls must be broken, because porous clay absorbs impurity in a way that cannot be washed out. Guzik notes the hygienic wisdom: if a rodent crawled into a bowl and died, breaking the bowl prevented transmission of disease. [Enduring Word on Lev 11:31–38](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-11/)

**v. 34 —** Any food that has had water come upon it (moistened) and any drink in a contaminated vessel become unclean. The moisture acts as a conductor of impurity.

**v. 35 —** Ovens and cooking stoves (or “covered pots” — see v. 32 note above) upon which a carcass falls must be smashed. They remain unclean.

**v. 36 —** A notable exception: a spring or cistern (a body of water with plenty of water) remains clean even if a carcass falls into it. However, the person who *touches* the carcass within the water still becomes unclean. The Pulpit Commentary does not elaborate on the rationale, but the distinction is that flowing or abundant water is not itself rendered unclean (unlike water in a small vessel). [Pulpit on Lev 11:31–38](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

**vv. 37–38 —** Dry seed for sowing remains clean if a carcass falls on it. But if water has been put on the seed (i.e., it is moistened), and then a carcass falls on it, the seed becomes unclean. The Pulpit Commentary explains: “the moisture would convey the corruption into the seeds.” [Pulpit on Lev 11:31–38](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

Guzik sums up the whole section: these laws “gave the Israelite household a reason to prevent pests and creeping things from coming into a house. No one wanted to destroy many earthen vessels and cooking tools or throw out a lot of food.” The regulations promoted general domestic cleanliness. [Enduring Word on Lev 11:31–38](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-11/)

---

## Verses 39–40: Carcasses of Clean Animals

**v. 39 —** The Cambridge Bible notes: “The carcase even of a clean beast causes uncleanness.” The Pulpit Commentary explains that the “loathsomeness of the bodies of even clean animals that have died a natural death” makes them convey defilement. These rules apply to animals that die naturally, not to animals properly slaughtered for food or sacrifice. [Pulpit on Lev 11:39–40](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html); [Cambridge Bible on Lev 11:39](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/leviticus/11.htm)

**v. 40 —** Three categories are distinguished: (a) eating from the carcass, (b) carrying it, and (c) touching it — all require washing clothes and uncleanness until evening. Ellicott notes that again the Second Temple interpreters understood “wash his clothes” to include bathing the body, though the text abbreviates. [Ellicott on Lev 11:25](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-11.html)

---

## Verses 41–43: Creeping Animals — Absolute Prohibition

**v. 41 —** “Every creeping thing that creeps on the earth shall be an abomination; it shall not be eaten.” The Pulpit Commentary identifies this as the final class: vermin, part of the un-winged creeping things already mentioned in vv. 29–30. Guzik adds that “in the Old Testament, the idea of an abomination is often linked to idolatry” — eating these creatures was considered not merely unhealthy but spiritually defiling and even idolatrous. [Pulpit on Lev 11:41–43](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html); [Enduring Word on Lev 11:41–43](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-11/)

**v. 42 —** Three categories of creeping things are specified by Ellicott: (1) “whatsoever goeth upon the belly” — serpents and serpentine worms (alluding to Genesis 3:14); (2) “whatsoever goeth upon all four” — creatures with four legs that move like reptiles, such as scorpions and beetles; (3) “whatsoever hath more feet” (or “many feet”) — creatures with numerous short legs, such as centipedes and caterpillars. [Ellicott on Lev 11:42](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-11.html)

The Pulpit Commentary categorises similarly: “goeth upon the belly” = snakes, worms, maggots; “goeth upon all four” = moles, rats, hedgehogs; “hath more feet” = centipedes, caterpillars, spiders. [Pulpit on Lev 11:41–43](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

A notable scribal detail: the Pulpit Commentary records that the Hebrew letter ו (*vav*) in the word גָּחוֹן (*gachon*, “belly”) in this verse is written in larger type, because Jewish scribal tradition identified this letter as the exact middle letter of the entire Pentateuch — a mark of the extreme care taken in preserving the text. [Pulpit on Lev 11:41–43](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

**v. 43 —** “Do not defile yourselves… do not become unclean or defiled by them.” Ellicott notes that the Hebrew term for “make yourselves abominable” (or “render yourselves detestable”) occurs only here and in Leviticus 20:25. Those who eat what is “abominable” become abominable themselves. [Ellicott on Lev 11:43](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-11.html)

---

## Verses 44–47: The Theological Purpose of the Dietary Laws

**v. 44 —** “For I am the LORD your God; consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, because I am holy.” The Pulpit Commentary states: these concluding verses “give a religious sanction to the previous regulations, and make them matters of sacred, not merely sanitary or political, obligation.” They teach that “ceremonial cleanness of the body was a symbol of holiness of heart, and a means of attaining to the latter.” [Pulpit on Lev 11:44–47](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

Ellicott adds: “As the Lord who is their God is Himself holy, His people, in order to enjoy perfect communion with Him, must also be holy. Hence they must abstain from all these objects of defilement which mar that holy communion.” He notes Peter’s quotation of this verse in 1 Peter 1:15–16. [Ellicott on Lev 11:44](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-11.html)

Guzik emphasises: “God claims the right to speak to every area of our life, including what we eat.” The dietary laws consecrated Israel — they set them apart from Gentile nations and made fellowship with non-believers far more difficult. He cites Daniel 1 as an example of the consecrating effect. [Enduring Word on Lev 11:44–47](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-11/)

**v. 45 —** “For I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt so that I would be your God; therefore be holy, because I am holy.” The Pulpit Commentary suggests Egypt may be specifically named “as being the land of animal-worship” — the dietary laws thus counteracted Egyptian religious influence. The key principle: “The only way by which there can be communion between God and man is the way of holiness.” [Pulpit on Lev 11:44–47](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

Guzik notes: “God had a claim to the obedience of the people of Israel because He was their redeemer. He freed them from 400 years of Egyptian slavery.” [Enduring Word on Lev 11:44–47](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-11/)

**v. 46 —** “This is the law regarding animals, birds, all living creatures that move in the water, and all creatures that crawl along the ground.” Ellicott observes an interesting structural point: the four classes are listed in a different order in this summary than in the chapter itself. The chapter order is: (1) land animals, (2) water animals, (3) birds, (4) swarming animals. The summary order is: (1) land animals, (2) birds, (3) water animals, (4) swarming animals. The same phenomenon occurs in the summary of the sacrificial law in Leviticus 7:37–38. The Cambridge Bible adds that the summary “refers only to the rules about eating, and so makes no reference to Leviticus 11:24–30” (the rules about touching carcasses). [Ellicott on Lev 11:46](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-11.html); [Cambridge Bible on Lev 11:46](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/leviticus/11.htm)

**v. 47 —** “You must distinguish between the unclean and the clean, between animals that may be eaten and those that may not.” Ellicott translates: “that ye may put difference” — the design of the dietary law is to enable both leaders and people to distinguish clean from unclean by the criteria specified.

He further records an intriguing Second Temple interpretation: because the same Hebrew word for “beast” is used for both the edible and non-edible animal, the rabbis concluded that even a *clean* animal might become inedible if it had organic defects or disease. They enacted the canon that an animal is “perfectly sound when it is capable of conceiving and bringing forth young.” This is why the Septuagint (LXX) renders “beast” here by a word meaning “viviparous.” [Ellicott on Lev 11:47](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-11.html)

Gill summarises: the first clause (“distinguish between the unclean and the clean”) covers all creatures generally; the second clause (“between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten”) instances the particular case of land animals, distinguished by the criteria of parted hoof and chewing the cud. [Gill on Lev 11:47](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/11-47.htm)

---

## Tradition-Specific Perspectives

### Reformed (Calvin)

John Calvin’s commentary, accessed via StudyLight.org, takes a strong position against the “health” interpretation of the dietary laws. He writes: “Those who imagine that God here had regard to their health, as if discharging the office of a Physician, pervert by their vain speculation the whole force and utility of this law.” For Calvin, the dietary laws were entirely ceremonial — “a part of that elementary instruction under which God kept His ancient people” — and their purpose was to teach spiritual purity through external symbols. The distinction of meats is abolished in Christ (Colossians 2:16; Romans 14:14). Calvin also addresses the apparent contradiction that clean/unclean distinctions existed before the Law (Noah): he argues the pre-Law distinction applied only to *sacrifices*, not to eating; before Moses, Abraham could lawfully eat swine’s flesh. [Calvin on Leviticus 11](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-11.html)

On the allegorical reading of cloven hoof (discernment) and chewing the cud (meditation), Calvin neither fully rejects nor endorses it: he says “I do not find any fault with, nor even refuse that which has been handed down from the ancients,” but warns against the “subtlety” of those who use it to justify fanciful interpretations. His simpler reading: the solid hoof signifies wildness; non-ruminating animals “feed for the most part on filth and excrement.” [Calvin on Lev 11:3](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-11.html)

On vv. 43–44, Calvin stresses that the main point is not health but that the Israelites “might know that nothing defiles a man except what comes out of his mouth” and that the external rules were means to “accustom them to study purity.” He laments that the Jews later satisfied themselves with “trifling observances” rather than pursuing the spiritual reality. [Calvin on Lev 11:43](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-11.html)

### Baptist (Garner-Howes)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary confirms that vv. 44–47 show “the primary purpose of the dietary regulations regarding clean and unclean were not solely for hygienic or sanitary purposes. They pictured that ceremonial cleanness symbolizes spiritual holiness.” On the Christian application: “There are no Scriptural sanctions against eating any of these creatures designated as ‘unclean’ in the Law, for God’s people today, Ac 10:9-15. However, it is suggested that it would be helpful to observe these restrictions, from a health standpoint, see Ro 15:4.” [Garner-Howes on Lev 11:41–47](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/leviticus-11.html) — This represents a distinctive Baptist note: the laws are not binding, but voluntary observance *may* be wise for health.

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik)

As noted throughout above, Guzik combines several lines of reasoning: hygienic benefit (protection from disease, the Black Death example), consecration/separation from Gentiles, testing of obedience, and the clear New Testament freedom from these laws (Acts 15; Colossians 2:16; 1 Timothy 4:1–5; Romans 14:14). He applies the principle to Christians: “we should recognize that while these specific dietary laws no longer apply to us as Christians, the principle behind them — that we consecrate ourselves and live with bodily discipline… remains a wise guide.” [Enduring Word on Lev 11](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-11/)

### Anglican/Pulpit Tradition

The Pulpit Commentary grounds the dietary laws in natural revulsion: “the prohibition to eat carnivorous and other animals repulsive to the taste is probably in accordance with the rules of health.” But its primary explanation is symbolic: “certain creatures were forbidden because they were offensive to the taste, and, being so offensive, they were symbolical of vicious things, which must be avoided, lest they make those that partake of them or touch them to become vicious like themselves.” The Pulpit Commentary thus bridges the hygienic and symbolic readings, unlike Calvin who rejects the health motive entirely. [Pulpit on Lev 11 Introduction](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-11.html)

---

## Summary of Key Theological Themes

| Theme | Source |
|---|---|
| Carrying a carcass is a higher defilement than mere touch (washing clothes required) | Ellicott, Gill, Cambridge |
| Pharisees vs. Sadducees: dispute over whether touching *living* unclean animals defiled | Ellicott |
| “Wash his clothes” = includes bathing the whole body (Second Temple interpretation) | Ellicott |
| Dietary laws primarily ceremonial/symbolic, not merely hygienic | Calvin, Pulpit, Garner-Howes |
| Hygienic benefit as a secondary blessing | Guzik, Pulpit, Garner-Howes |
| The laws consecrated Israel and separated them from Gentiles | Guzik, Calvin, Pulpit |
| Christians are not bound by these laws (Acts 10; 15; Col 2; 1 Tim 4; Rom 14) | Guzik, Calvin, Garner-Howes |
| Holiness is the ultimate purpose: “Be holy, for I am holy” (vv. 44–45) | All sources |
| The summary (vv. 46–47) reorders the classes and covers only eating rules, not carcass-touching | Ellicott, Cambridge |
